body_markdown:
# How to Transfer Credit Card Points to Airlines: The Complete Guide


The same 60,000 points that book a $600 economy seat through a credit card portal can book a business class seat that sells for $6,000. The only thing standing between those two outcomes is a transfer, and most people holding points have never made one.


Learning how to transfer credit card points to airlines is the highest-value skill in award travel. Portal bookings pay a fixed rate, typically 1 to 1.5 cents per point ([Forbes Advisor](https://www.forbes.com/advisor/credit-cards/travel-rewards/different-points-program-comparison/) ). Moved into the right airline program, those same points commonly reach 2 to 20 times that.


The part nobody explains well is the middle. You have probably read that transferring beats the portal. What you have not been told is which of your point balances can reach a given airline, how long the move takes, and that once it is done it can never be undone.


This guide covers all of it: which programs transfer to which airlines, how fast each one moves, when a transfer beats the portal and when it does not, and the one rule that protects you from an expensive mistake.


At Pointhound, we search 21 loyalty programs and 200+ airlines across 75,000+ routes at once, so you can see which program books a given seat, and at what point cost, before you move anything.


## What Is a Credit Card Transfer Partner, and Why Does Transferring Beat the Portal?


A transfer partner is an airline loyalty program that your credit card points can move into. Transferring beats the portal because airlines price seats in miles, not in cents.


Five card programs let you do this: Chase Ultimate Rewards, American Express Membership Rewards, Capital One, Citi ThankYou and Bilt Rewards. Points in these programs are called **transferable points** , because they are not stuck with one airline. An airline-branded card earns miles locked to that single airline. Transferable points can go to any partner on the list.


The exchange rate is called a ratio. A 1:1 ratio means 1,000 of your points becomes 1,000 airline miles, which is the standard across most partners. It is not universal, though, and the exceptions are worth knowing before you press the button.

Capital One JetBlue TrueBlue 5:3 600 points

Amex JetBlue TrueBlue 250:200 800 points

Ratios from[Capital One](https://www.capitalone.com/learn-grow/money-management/venture-miles-transfer-partnerships/) ,[Bankrate on Amex](https://www.bankrate.com/credit-cards/rewards/american-express-transfer-partners/) and[Bankrate on Citi](https://www.bankrate.com/credit-cards/rewards/citi-transfer-partners/) .


Now the value logic. A credit card portal pays a fixed rate per point. The[Consumer Financial Protection Bureau](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_credit-card-rewards_issue-spotlight_2024-05.pdf) puts it bluntly: a point's value varies by redemption option, but issuers themselves typically estimate it at about a cent. The same report notes that issuer earnings forecasts often assume cardholders will not redeem the full value of what they earn.


An airline does not price seats that way. It publishes a mile cost per cabin, and that cost does not rise with the cash fare. That gap is where 2 to 20 times the portal value lives, roughly 10x in business class and 20x in first. We break the full comparison down in our guide to[the credit card portal versus transferring points](https://www.pointhound.com/blog/credit-card-portal-vs-transferring-points) .

Issuers group a few entries differently, so a tally of one column will not always match a published partner count.


Read across the rows and one program stands out. **Air France-KLM Flying Blue is the only airline program in the table that takes points from all five card programs.** Virgin Atlantic, Singapore KrisFlyer, Avianca LifeMiles and Air Canada Aeroplan each take points from four of the five. Learn those first, because whatever you hold, you can reach them.


The scarce ones matter just as much. United MileagePlus is reachable only through Chase and Bilt. American AAdvantage only through Citi, and only on two of its cards. Delta SkyMiles only through Amex, and Alaska's Atmos Rewards only through Bilt. If you want to fly one of those airlines on points, the card in your wallet decides whether you can.


### Chase Ultimate Rewards Transfer Partners


Chase reaches 10 airline programs, all at 1:1, and moves points only in increments of 1,000. Transfers are available only from the Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve and Ink Business Preferred ([Chase](https://www.chase.com/personal/credit-cards/education/basics/how-to-transfer-chase-ultimate-rewards-points) ). It is the shortest list of the five, and[NerdWallet](https://www.nerdwallet.com/travel/learn/chase-transfer-partners-guide) counts it the same way.


Short is not the same as weak. Chase is one of only two programs that reaches United MileagePlus, and one of only two that reaches Southwest. For the full guide, see[Chase Ultimate Rewards](https://www.pointhound.com/blog/chase-ultimate-rewards-how-to-use-your-points-for-maximum-flight-value) .


### Amex Membership Rewards Transfer Partners


Seventeen airline programs, nearly all at 1:1, with Aeromexico at 1,000:1,600 and JetBlue at 250:200 ([Bankrate](https://www.bankrate.com/credit-cards/rewards/american-express-transfer-partners/) ).


Two of those partners exist nowhere else in the table: Delta SkyMiles and ANA Mileage Club. Amex also runs transfer bonuses of 10% to 50% a few times a year ([Forbes Advisor](https://www.forbes.com/advisor/credit-cards/travel-rewards/different-points-program-comparison/) ), which is a real argument for waiting rather than transferring today. Our full guide to[Amex Membership Rewards](https://www.pointhound.com/blog/amex-membership-rewards-how-to-get-the-most-value) goes deeper.


### Capital One Transfer Partners


Capital One reaches 18 airline programs. Fourteen transfer at 1:1, Emirates, EVA Air and Japan Airlines at 2:1.5, and JetBlue at 5:3. You need at least 1,000 miles to transfer, and the name on the loyalty account has to match the name on the Capital One account ([Capital One](https://www.capitalone.com/learn-grow/money-management/venture-miles-transfer-partnerships/) ).


Finnair Plus is the one you will not find anywhere else among the five. Read our full guide to[Capital One Venture miles](https://www.pointhound.com/blog/capital-one-venture-miles-maximize-value-for-flights) for the rest.


### Citi ThankYou Transfer Partners


Citi is the only one of the five that reaches American AAdvantage, and it carries Thai Airways, which nobody else on this list does. The catch is that your ratio depends entirely on which card you hold.


Across its 15 airline programs, the Citi Strata Elite and Citi Strata Premier transfer at 1:1. Every other ThankYou card transfers at 1,000:700, so 1,000 points becomes 700 miles, and American AAdvantage is off the table entirely ([Bankrate](https://www.bankrate.com/credit-cards/rewards/citi-transfer-partners/) ,[Citi](https://www.citi.com/credit-cards/money-management/citi-thankyou-rewards-faqs) ). Check which card you actually hold before you plan around a Citi transfer.


### Bilt Rewards Transfer Partners


Nineteen airline programs, every single one at 1:1, which is the cleanest ratio structure of the five. Minimums depend on status: 2,000 points at Blue, 1,000 at Silver, Gold or Platinum, always in 1,000-point increments ([Bilt](https://support.biltrewards.com/hc/en-us/articles/19086448638989-Bilt-s-Transfer-Partners) ). Bilt is the only program in the table that reaches Atmos Rewards, the combined Alaska and Hawaiian program, and the only one that reaches Spirit. It is also the second route into United, alongside Chase.


## How Long Do Credit Card Point Transfers Take?


Most transfers are instant. A minority take longer, and every issuer publishes a maximum that runs far past the typical experience.


The maximums below are each program's stated policy, not the wait you should expect. Bankrate, walking through an Amex transfer step by step, notes that while certain partners can take up to 48 hours, most transfers land instantly.


Points program Typical speed Published maximum


Amex Membership Rewards Instant for nearly every airline partner ANA Mileage Club: up to 48 hours


Bilt Rewards Immediate in most cases Up to 48 hours, and up to 72 hours for Southwest


Capital One Several partners transfer instantly Not published


Chase Ultimate Rewards Most process by the next business day Up to 7 business days


Citi ThankYou Not all transfers are instant Up to one week


Sources:[Bankrate on Amex](https://www.bankrate.com/credit-cards/rewards/american-express-transfer-partners/) ,[Bilt](https://support.biltrewards.com/hc/en-us/articles/19086448638989-Bilt-s-Transfer-Partners) ,[Forbes Advisor on Capital One](https://www.forbes.com/advisor/credit-cards/travel-rewards/different-points-program-comparison/) ,[Chase](https://www.chase.com/personal/credit-cards/education/basics/how-to-transfer-chase-ultimate-rewards-points) and[Bankrate on Citi](https://www.bankrate.com/credit-cards/rewards/citi-transfer-partners/) .


Minimums and increments belong in the same mental note. Chase moves points only in increments of 1,000. Capital One requires at least 1,000 miles. Bilt requires 2,000 points at Blue status and 1,000 at Silver and above, always in 1,000-point increments.


Timing matters more than it looks. Award seats are inventory, and inventory disappears. If your transfer is one of the slow ones and the seat sells while your points are in transit, you are left holding miles you never planned to hold. That is the second reason to confirm the award is live before you move anything. The first reason is worse.


## The One Rule That Matters: Transfers Only Go One Way


A point transfer cannot be reversed. Once your points become airline miles they belong to that airline's program and follow its rules, and no issuer will move them back.


Every major issuer says so plainly, in its own words:


- Chase: "point transfers to travel partners are final" ([Chase](https://www.chase.com/personal/credit-cards/education/basics/how-to-transfer-chase-ultimate-rewards-points) )
- Amex: "all transfers are final" ([American Express](https://www.americanexpress.com/us/customer-service/faq.transfer-membership-reward-points.html) )
- Capital One: "there's no way to transfer miles back into your Capital One rewards account once the transfer is finalized" ([Capital One](https://www.capitalone.com/learn-grow/money-management/venture-miles-transfer-partnerships/) )
- Bilt: "Once points are transferred, they cannot be reversed" ([Bilt](https://support.biltrewards.com/hc/en-us/articles/19086448638989-Bilt-s-Transfer-Partners) )


The[CFPB](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_credit-card-rewards_issue-spotlight_2024-05.pdf) collected what that means in practice. In one complaint, a cardholder transferred points, could not book the award because of technical problems on the airline's site, and asked her bank to reverse it. The dispute failed.


> Customers "literally have no protection at all after they initiate a transfer."


Two smaller costs come with transfers. Moving points into a US-based airline program such as Delta SkyMiles or JetBlue TrueBlue can carry a federal excise tax, a government fee charged on the transfer itself ([Bankrate](https://www.bankrate.com/credit-cards/rewards/american-express-transfer-partners/) ). And transferring the week before a bonus is money left behind, since Amex runs 10% to 50% transfer bonuses a few times a year.


So the rule: **confirm the award seat is bookable, then transfer, then book.** Never any other order. Amex's own instructions tell you to check availability and the points required before transferring ([American Express](https://www.americanexpress.com/us/customer-service/faq.transfer-membership-reward-points.html) ), and[Bilt](https://support.biltrewards.com/hc/en-us/articles/19086448638989-Bilt-s-Transfer-Partners) recommends confirming availability and putting the reservation on hold first.


This is the exact risk a cross-program search removes. Pointhound shows the live award, which loyalty program books it, and what it costs in points, before a single point moves.


## When a Transfer Beats the Portal, and When It Does Not


Transfer when the airline's mile price beats the portal's point price for the same seat, which is nearly always true in premium cabins.


The reverse case is real too, and worth taking seriously. Use the portal when award space does not exist on your route, when the math runs the other way, or when you need the trip locked in today.


Transfer when:


- The cabin is business or first. This is where the 2 to 20 times range lives, roughly 10x in[business class](https://www.pointhound.com/blog/how-to-find-cheap-business-class-flights-with-points) and 20x in[first](https://www.pointhound.com/blog/how-to-fly-first-class-with-points) .
- The award seat is confirmed live, on your route and your date.
- The mile price, after the ratio, comes in under what the portal would charge you in points.


Use the portal when:


- There is no award seat on the route or date you need. A great redemption you cannot book is worth nothing.
- The trip is a cheap domestic economy fare. The portal's fixed rate is competitive there, and the points you save are better spent on a premium cabin later.
- You need certainty today.


For scale, award prices start lower than most beginners expect. US domestic economy awards can start around 4,000 miles one way, and economy to Europe from around 6,000, with a typical Europe transfer running 20,000 to 40,000 miles. Those are starting points on the best routes, not what every seat costs.


Two more things to know. A portal booking is a paid ticket, so it earns frequent flyer miles like any other fare. And award bookings can sometimes earn miles too, because some programs credit them. The full side-by-side lives in our guide to[the credit card portal versus transferring points](https://www.pointhound.com/blog/credit-card-portal-vs-transferring-points) .


## How to Transfer Credit Card Points to an Airline, Step by Step


Find the award seat first, confirm which program books it, link your loyalty account, transfer the exact number of points, then book with the airline.


1. **Know what you hold and what it reaches.** Add up your Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi and Bilt balances, then check them against the table above. If points are new to you entirely, start with[how to book flights with credit card points](https://www.pointhound.com/blog/how-to-book-flights-with-credit-card-points) .
2. **Find the live award seat before anything else.** Checking airline sites one at a time is where beginners lose seats, because by the time you reach the fifth program the first one has changed. Pointhound searches 200+ airlines and 21 loyalty programs across 75,000+ routes in a single query and returns which program books each seat, what it costs in points, and step-by-step booking instructions. You book directly with the airline.
3. **Check the ratio, the minimum and the fee before you commit.** Confirm the ratio is what you think it is, that you clear the program's minimum, and whether a federal excise tax applies, which it can on transfers into US airline programs such as Delta SkyMiles and JetBlue TrueBlue.
4. **Link your airline loyalty account to your card program.** Names have to match exactly. Capital One requires the loyalty account name to match the Capital One account name, and Amex requires the two accounts to be linked before any transfer can be made. Create the airline account first if you do not have one.
5. **Transfer only what the booking needs, then book immediately.** Move the exact amount, in whatever increments the program requires, and complete the booking the moment the miles land. Most transfers are instant, but the published maximums run to a week on some programs, and a held reservation is safer than a fast transfer.
6. **Let alerts do the waiting.** When the seat is not there today,[Pointhound Flight Alerts](https://www.pointhound.com/alerts) track 70,000+ routes and notify you by SMS or email the moment award space opens on a route you are watching.[Deal Discovery emails](https://www.pointhound.com/digest) match curated award releases to the programs you hold and the airports you fly from.


The whole sequence reduces to four words: search first, transfer last.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Can you transfer credit card points back from an airline?


No. Every major program states that transfers are final. Chase, Amex, Capital One and Bilt all say points cannot be moved back once transferred, and the airline program's rules govern them from that moment. Confirm the award seat is bookable before you transfer anything.


### How long do credit card point transfers take?


Most are instant. The documented exceptions: ANA through Amex can take up to 48 hours, Bilt asks for up to 48 hours and up to 72 for Southwest, Chase states transfers may take up to 7 business days, and Citi says not all transfers are instant and some take up to one week.


### Which credit card has the most airline transfer partners?


Bilt reaches 19 airline programs, Capital One 18, Amex 17, Citi 15 and Chase 10. Count is not the same as usefulness. Chase has the fewest partners but is one of only two programs that reaches United, and only Citi reaches American AAdvantage.


### Do all points transfer at a 1:1 ratio?


Most do, but not all. Capital One sends 2 points for 1.5 miles to Emirates, EVA Air and Japan Airlines, and 5 for 3 to JetBlue. Amex sends 250 points for 200 JetBlue points. Citi pays 1:1 only on Strata Elite and Strata Premier cards, and 1,000:700 on others.


### Is it always better to transfer points than use the credit card portal?


No. Transferring wins on premium cabins and on any route where the airline's mile price beats the portal's point price, which is common but not universal. When there is no award seat on your date, or the route is a cheap domestic economy fare, the portal is the better tool.


### What is the minimum number of points I can transfer?


It depends on the program. Chase transfers in increments of 1,000 points, Capital One requires at least 1,000 miles, and Bilt requires 2,000 points at Blue status or 1,000 at Silver and above, always in 1,000-point increments.


## Key Takeaways


- A transfer partner is an airline loyalty program your credit card points move into, and transferring is where points stop being worth a fixed 1 to 1.5 cents and start being worth 2 to 20 times that.
- Chase reaches 10 airline programs, Amex 17, Capital One 18, Citi 15 and Bilt 19. Most transfer at 1:1.
- Air France-KLM Flying Blue is the only airline program that takes points from all five card programs. Virgin Atlantic, Singapore KrisFlyer, Avianca LifeMiles and Air Canada Aeroplan each take points from four of the five.
- United MileagePlus is reachable only through Chase and Bilt, American AAdvantage only through Citi, Delta SkyMiles only through Amex, and Alaska's Atmos Rewards only through Bilt.
- Most transfers are instant, but published maximums run from 48 hours to a full week depending on the program.
- Point transfers cannot be reversed. Chase, Amex, Capital One and Bilt each say so in their own terms, and the CFPB has documented cardholders left with no recourse afterward.
- Confirm the award seat is live and bookable before transferring. That single habit prevents almost every expensive mistake in award travel, and transfers into US airline programs can carry a federal excise tax on top.


## The Transfer Is the Easy Part


Transferring points is not an advanced move. It is one screen inside a card account, a few clicks, and usually an instant result. The hard part is everything that has to be true before you click: that the seat exists, that your program can book it, and that the mile price is worth the points you are about to spend.
